2021_187_tsd_equity_and_inclusion_board_.paragraph: A twenty-slide Troy School District presentation titled "TSD Equity & Inclusion," delivered as a Board of Education workshop on May 18, 2021, tracing the district's equity work from the 2009 TSD Diversity Study to a newly created Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships position built around three priorities: Assess, Connect and Engage. The centerpiece finding is from the Equity & Inclusion Survey conducted by Hannover Research, which captured 7,448 stakeholder perceptions and identified the greatest opportunity for improvement in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents.
2021_187_tsd_equity_and_inclusion_board_.page:
**Framing**
Presented under the title "TSD Equity & Inclusion" as a Board of Education workshop item for the meeting of May 18, 2021. Twenty slides, authored around five guiding principles attributed to Cornelius Godfrey.

**Guiding Principles**
1. Radical Equity: dismantling systems of inequity takes courage, imagination and a high tolerance for discomfort.
2. Gracious Inclusion: invitations to "the table" extended not on the basis of perceived merit, but because it's time to eat.
3. Abundance Mentality: belief that available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child, everyday.
4. Fearless Feedback: an honest look at ourselves and actively seeking critique, without threat of reprisal.
5. Many Hands: the work can never be "my work," "your work" or "their work" — it must always be "our work."

**Where we've been**
The 2009 TSD Diversity Study, conducted by R&J Consulting Group (Rosalind Cox), produced findings and recommendations in four areas: Personnel Diversity (review hiring and recruiting practices with a focus on retention), Cultural Awareness (appoint a Diversity Council, establish staff-wide competencies and incorporate them into evaluation), Curriculum (review data for gaps in achievement and access; review materials for inclusivity), and Parent Outreach (establish parent networks). A Diversity Council convened meetings between 2011 and 2012.

**Where we are**

| Initiative | Participants |
| --- | --- |
| National Equity Project | District and building administrators, teachers, students |
| Teacher's College: TRWP | Teachers |
| Book Clubs | Elementary and secondary teachers, administrators, support staff |
| Excellence in Equity Statement | Board of Education |
| Leading for Equity | Teachers, support staff (early adopters) |
| Building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching | Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools |
| Equity Survey by Hannover Research | All stakeholders (staff, students, parents) |

**Where we're going**
System-wide integration across all pillars, departments and content areas, with significant investment from Teaching & Learning; community voice through collaborative meetings and quantitative evidence; creation of a new Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships role with three priorities; and an equity agenda calling for a comprehensive framework of supports at building and district levels (BELE), a learning continuum for all TSD employees, capacity building through stakeholder partnerships, transparency and reporting mechanisms, and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

**Survey results**

| Respondent group | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Students (grades 5-12) | 5,520 |
| Parents | 1,503 |
| TSD staff members | 425 |
| Total stakeholder perceptions reflected | 7,448 |

Key finding: the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. The final report was expected in late May or early June. Slides compare overall stakeholder perceptions against Black stakeholders, and overall parent perception against Black parents.

**Connecting**
Focused conversations with community members; Michigan Seal of Biliteracy; 70 scheduled connections via Calendly; an affinity group for TSD employees of color; postings shared to HBCUs via Handshake; MI Roundtable connections.

**Learning continuum**
A "house analogy" positions employees along three stages — Listening, Learning, Leading — described as a non-judgmental method of placing TSD employees along the continuum of learning for equity and inclusion.
2021_187_tsd_equity_and_inclusion_board_.verbose:
**Document and occasion**

A Troy School District PowerPoint presentation of twenty slides titled "TSD Equity & Inclusion," prepared for an Equity and Inclusion Board Workshop held in connection with the Board of Education meeting of May 18, 2021. It narrates the district's equity history, current initiatives, survey results, planned structure, and a staff learning continuum.

**Guiding Principles**

Five numbered principles are presented, attributed on the slide to Cornelius Godfrey. Radical Equity holds that the work of dismantling systems of inequity takes courage, imagination and a high tolerance for discomfort. Gracious Inclusion states that invitations to "the table" are extended not on the basis of perceived merit, but because it is time to eat. Abundance Mentality asserts that to effectively engage in the work of equity one must believe available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child, everyday. Fearless Feedback holds that achieving equity requires an honest look at ourselves and actively seeking critique, without the threat of reprisal. Many Hands states that improving outcomes for the marginalized means the effort can never be "my work," "your work" or "their work" — it must always be "our work."

**Where we've been**

The historical anchor is the 2009 TSD Diversity Study conducted by R&J Consulting Group, with Rosalind Cox named as the consultant. A Diversity Council convened meetings between 2011 and 2012. The study's findings and recommendations are grouped into four areas. Personnel Diversity: review hiring and recruiting practices with a focus on retention. Cultural Awareness: appoint a Diversity Council, establish staff-wide competencies and incorporate them into the evaluation process. Curriculum: review data to identify gaps in achievement and access, and review materials for inclusivity. Parent Outreach: establish parent networks to review concerns and recommendations.

**Where we are**

Current initiatives are paired with the audiences engaged in each. The National Equity Project involves district and building administrators, teachers and students. Teacher's College TRWP involves teachers. Book Clubs involve elementary and secondary teachers, administrators and support staff. The Excellence in Equity Statement is attributed to the Board of Education. Leading for Equity involves teachers and support staff described as early adopters. Building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching is associated with Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools. The Equity Survey by Hannover Research reaches all stakeholders — staff, students and parents.

**Where we're going and what's different now**

Five forward-looking themes are listed. System-wide integration means a place in all pillars, departments and content areas, with significant investment from Teaching & Learning. Community Voice covers collaborative meetings and quantitative evidence to support the work. The creation of a new equity role — Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships — carries three priorities: Assess, Connect and Engage. The Equity Agenda calls for implementing a comprehensive framework of supports at the building and district levels, identified as BELE; establishing a learning continuum for all TSD employees; building capacity for equity leadership through stakeholder partnerships; transparency and reporting mechanisms; and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

**Three Priorities in detail**

Assess: establish a baseline for current equity, inclusion and community relations; center the perspectives of marginalized stakeholders; gauge efficacy and implementation fidelity regularly. Connect: build dynamic stakeholder coalitions; empower stakeholders to advance equity and inclusion within their various spheres of influence; elevate the voices of marginalized students and families. Engage: focused action oriented toward positive outcomes for marginalized students and families; proactively respond to community concerns; enact practices aimed at systematizing equity and inclusion. Three source citations are footnoted: Bustamante, R. and J. Nelson, "The School-Wide Cultural Competence Checklist," 2007, at cnx.org; "Recommendations for Diversity Training," Arlington Public Schools, at apsva.us; and "Strategies for Promoting Culturally Responsive Classrooms," Alexandria City Public Schools, page 14, at acps.k12.va.us/equity/strategies.

**The Pulley Analogy**

A slide frames assessment, connections and engagement through a pulley. Assessment represents an accurate understanding of the size, weight and dimensions of the load. Connections are represented by the pulley itself, used to multiply and change the direction of effort. Engagement represents the work being done, aided by the mechanical and relational advantage of the pulley. A note adds that the work of advancing equity and inclusion must always be focused on improved outcomes for marginalized individuals and community members, and that efforts with no observable positive impact on the marginalized may be necessary as prerequisites for the work but are not themselves the work.

**Planned activities under each priority**

Under Assess: a comprehensive "Listening Tour" using qualitative methods (surveys, interviews, questionnaires, focus groups) and quantitative methods (a data deep dive for disparities in perceptions, discipline and academic outcomes), a community connections review, and a curriculum review. Under Connect: assemble a Community Advisory Board and a Student Advisory Board; develop a staff coalition district-wide and at building, subject-area and administration levels; establish feedback channels for staff and students; and partner with equity and inclusion exemplars at the district and ISD level. Under Engage: draft vision and mission statements; implement an accountability and transparency platform; develop a three-to-five-year strategic plan for equity and inclusion; develop research-based criteria for equity and inclusion; provide professional development; and establish norms for dialogue.

**Equity & Inclusion Survey results**

The assessment slide reports that the Equity & Inclusion Survey reflected 7,448 stakeholder perceptions, comprising 5,520 students in grades 5 through 12, 1,503 parents and 425 TSD staff members. The stated key finding is that the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. The final report was expected in late May or early June. Two subsequent slides are given over to comparisons: overall stakeholder perceptions versus Black stakeholders, and overall parent perception versus Black parents.

**Connecting activity to date**

Reported connection work includes focused conversations with community members, the Michigan Seal of Biliteracy, 70 scheduled connections via Calendly, an affinity group for TSD employees of color, job postings shared to HBCUs via Handshake, and MI Roundtable connections.

**Equity & Inclusion Learning Continuum**

The final section presents a Troy School District learning continuum with three stages — Listening, Learning, Leading — introduced through a house analogy described as a non-judgmental method of positioning TSD employees along the continuum of learning for equity and inclusion. Listening involves examining practice for compliance with district equity and inclusion standards, establishing a working knowledge of key terms and definitions, and considering available on-ramps for additional learning. Learning involves reflection on practice to implement cultural competencies, taking responsibility for professional learning, identifying and confronting personal biases, and understanding the role of culture and identity in learning. Leading involves reflection on systems and practices, identifying equity challenges, analyzing data for disparities, and taking responsibility for the learning of others within one's sphere of influence.

**Continuum examples**

Listening examples include following district policy for course recommendation, completing an online training module on cultural competence, reviewing evaluation criteria with a direct supervisor, reading context-specific articles focused on equity, inclusion or diversity, and reviewing policies released by neighboring districts relating to equity and anti-racism. Learning examples include participating in a district-sponsored book study, viewing a documentary film and participating in a discussion group, attending trainings offered by TSD or other local organizations, designating an accountability partner to encourage engagement and learning, and engaging in county-level organizations with equity as a central focus. Leading examples include participating in the district's Leading for Equity learning series, developing systems of group reflection and accountability, leading discussion groups and book clubs to support learning and growth, identifying and addressing system-level barriers to equitable access and practice, and adopting policies that advance equitable and anti-racist practices.
